conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really nauseous since this morning and I’ve thrown up a few times. It’s been hard to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of gastroparesis, right? That’s when the stomach doesn’t empty properly, often due to diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I have Type 1 diabetes and my stomach has always been slow. I have a gastric pacemaker to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, and we checked — your pacemaker looks intact on the X-ray. No changes. We also did a chest X-ray because we saw something unclear in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh? Is something wrong with my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. There was a faint shadow near your shoulder blade, but it might just be how you were positioned. A repeat X-ray showed clear lungs. So we think it’s nothing serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might be pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We also checked your heart enzymes because your initial ones were a bit high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heart enzymes? Do I have heart damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. Your first CK-MB was elevated, but we repeated the test — it’s now normal. Troponin, which is more specific for heart injury, was always negative. So it’s likely a lab anomaly, not a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I don’t have chest pain or anything, so that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Right now, your main issue is the gastroparesis flare. We’re giving you IV fluids and anti-nausea meds like Zofran and Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel a little better since the shot in the ER. But why did this happen now? I didn’t change my diet or insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes these flares happen without a clear trigger. Stress, blood sugar swings, or even just the chronic nerve damage from diabetes can cause it. Your blood sugar was 238 in the ER — a bit high, but not extreme.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my sugars have been running in the 200s lately, even though I’m not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with gastroparesis. We’ve been giving you insulin on a sliding scale here, and your sugars have been much better — in the 100s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So should I adjust my insulin at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your insulin the same for now. But we are starting you on two new medications: a baby aspirin daily and a low-dose lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why aspirin and lisinopril? I don’t have heart or kidney problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With long-term Type 1 diabetes, we use these to prevent complications. Aspirin helps protect your heart, and lisinopril protects your kidneys, especially if there’s early signs of damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. I didn’t know I needed that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Just checking in. How’s the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since I got here. Still feel a little queasy, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to try advancing your diet — start with clear liquids and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Small sips at first. We’ll watch you closely. If you keep it down, we’ll move to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without vomiting. You’re on a soft diet now — how are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had some applesauce and toast this morning and it stayed down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll keep the IV fluids running for now but plan to switch you back to oral meds soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aiming for discharge in a couple of days. We want to make sure you’re tolerating a regular diet and your blood sugars stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. You’re doing well. You’ve had a regular meal and kept it down. Your blood sugar is 112 — perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel almost back to normal. Can I stop the IV now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll remove the IV today. You’ll go back to your regular insulin — glargine at night and lispro as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new pills — aspirin and lisinopril — I take those every day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. One baby aspirin daily, and half a lisinopril tablet once a day. We’ll increase it slowly if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have lorazepam and Phenergan to take as needed if nausea comes back. But try to avoid overusing them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the nurse said something about my gastric pacemaker being checked later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Dr. Patel will check it as an outpatient. It looks fine now, but we want to make sure it’s working optimally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days without vomiting and you’re eating normally. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea comes back and you can’t keep fluids down, or if you develop fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing, call your doctor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your endocrinologist in a week. And Dr. Patel will schedule the pacemaker check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. You’re stable, tolerating food, and your labs are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your new meds daily, monitor your sugars, and call if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Have a safe trip home.
